We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{3}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{e}^{x}]}_{a}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{3}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/115e3198226940a76b770f5942bb06e6496bd234d6cb5fee2d33f19038931bd3.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{3}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{3}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
